1.pericope_label: I Paul myself beseech you: walking in the flesh but not warring after it

schools.summary: Place the chapter where the discourse turns, the Apostle having finished with almsgiving and shown that he loves more than he is loved, and now opportunely entering on points that involve more of reproof, with allusion to the false apostles.

Say that he proceeds partly to refute the calumnies with which he had been defamed and partly to repress the insolence of persons who could not bear restraint, both having construed his vehemence to the destruction of his authority; report that some think the discourse incomplete, the request never being expressed, and prefer that what was wanting in the former clause is completed here; concede that they were in the body, in a state of imperfection, attended with weaknesses and surrounded with afflictions, and in that sense walked in the flesh, while denying the charge itself; and call it a concession of no service to his adversaries, since being shut up in the prison of the body did not prevent the Spirit from showing itself marvellously in his weakness.

Hear mildness in the address, the Apostle speaking in a very mild and humble manner and plainly desirous that no occasion be given him to use severity, and note that where at the opening of the letter he had joined another with himself he now speaks only for himself.

Hear the same meekness, the entreaty being after the gentleness of Christ though he might have commanded, and take the emphatic form for an answer to a charge that he was base when present; reconstruct the charge itself, that it is customary for cowards and overbearing men to threaten the weak when present, to bluster when absent and to be obsequious before the strong; turn the denial into defiance, since he does not act the coward as they insinuate, having a good cause, a good captain, strength at will and courage at hand; and note that the plural is used for modesty and decency though he principally means himself.

Call it the third part of the epistle, in which he vigorously defends himself against a stubborn minority, adding that great ministers have passed through such trials ever since; hear instead a suppressed indignation showing itself in keen incisive irony, the opening formula being reserved for exceptionally strong emotion, with an implied warning almost a menace in the entreaty; notice that the verb for beseech changes between the two verses; put the distinction sharply, that walking in the flesh is a very different thing from walking by the standards of the flesh, which is what the enemies charged, since it is easy enough to make insinuations; give the usage, that the first phrase means the simple fact of bodily existence with its infirmities and commonly implies no sin where the second does; and say that no exemption is claimed from the common wants and frailties of nature.

debates: What tone the opening entreaty strikes.
Whether the sentence at the second verse is left incomplete.
What distinguishes walking in the flesh from warring after it.
Why the Apostle writes in the plural.
outliers: Ellicott alone hears suppressed indignation and keen incisive irony where Henry and Wesley hear meekness.
Robertson alone notices that the word for beseech is changed between the two verses.
Clarke alone reconstructs the charge as blustering when absent and obsequious when present.
Calvin alone reports and then rejects the view that the sentence is left unfinished.
Chrysostom alone marks this as the point where the discourse turns to reproof.

4.pericope_label: The weapons of our warfare: strong holds cast down, and disobedience avenged

schools.summary: Restrict the warfare to what is peculiar to ministers of the gospel, the ministerial office and its discharge, rather than the warfare common to all believers; keep the imaginations to the carnal reasonings of natural men against God and against every truth of the gospel, all disproved and silenced by the preaching of the word; take the vengeance not of the temporal sword but of the spiritual, censures and excommunication used with the suffrage of the church, or rather the extraordinary power an apostle held; observe that the warfare corresponds to the kind of weapons, the character of the one following from the other by an argument from contraries; read the movement as a change of subject, from the conflict with what rises in opposition to the ordinary preparation by which men are brought into subjection, since so long as we rest in our own judgment we are not subject at all; and say the power was given not merely to constrain voluntary disciples but to inflict something on the rebellious.

Note that the metaphor of a campaign is often used of the life and trials of a minister, and identify the carnal weapons with what the opposing party actually did, calumniating the Apostle, traducing the truth and preaching licentious doctrine; go at the Greek moral systems directly, since the philosophers valued themselves on schemes whose reasoning appeared conclusive while the principles assumed either did not exist or were false, as their whole mythology evidently was; narrow the armoury, granting that faith and prayer belong to it but judging the word of God chiefly intended; press the next phrase, that the thought taken captive is rather the faculty of the mind, which being overcome lays down all authority of its own; include both spiritual censure and miraculous punishment in the vengeance; and give two reasons for its delay, that they must first discountenance these men entirely, and that the sound part must give proof of obedience so that the innocent are not punished with the guilty.

Call the phrase essentially military and point to its use in the Greek version for the capture and destruction of fortresses, the weapons being the energies of spiritual powers given by the Eternal Spirit; list what they are not, neither eloquence nor talent nor learning nor wealth nor any external advantage men rely on; report the textual point that the noun is campaign and not army as some copies have it, both forms occurring in the papyri; take the word cast down in the sense of device and refer it to the systems of false philosophy, so entrenched as to be called the stronghold of God's enemies; make the connection that the noun is formed from the very verb used earlier of what the opponents reckoned about him, so that thoughts or reckonings would better carry the continuity; keep the siege in view, the reasonings being forts to be taken; gloss the idiom for readiness and the rare word for disobedience, which means to hear amiss or refuse to heed; and hear a qualification in the text itself, the following words implying that the opening ones were too unqualified.

debates: Whose warfare is in view — every believer's or the minister's only.
What the imaginations are that are cast down.
By what instrument the disobedience is to be avenged.
Why the punishment waits upon their obedience.
outliers: Gill alone restricts the warfare to the ministerial office.
Ellicott alone ties the word for imaginations back to the verb used of the charge against the Apostle.
Clarke alone attacks the Greek moral systems for assuming principles that did not exist or were false.
Wesley alone explains the delay as avoiding the punishment of the innocent with the guilty.
Robertson alone reports the variation between campaign and army in the manuscripts.

7.pericope_label: Do ye look on things after the outward appearance? Authority, boasting, and letters

schools.summary: Set out every ambiguity before choosing, since the phrase may mean the reality itself or an outward mask that deceives, the sentence may be read interrogatively or affirmatively, and the verb may be imperative or indicative; hear the clause as irony and a reproof for judging by appearance, listing what they judged by — the meanness of his person, the weakness of his body, the lowness of his voice, his poverty and afflictions; measure the boast against the field, since to claim greater authority than the false apostles or even than true ministers in common would still not exceed the bounds of truth and modesty; find the modesty in the earlier plural, by which he put himself among those he greatly excelled without leaving his authority impaired; say plainly that something is wanting in the broken sentence and fill it with a refusal, that he forbears the boast and drops the subject; and give the taunt in the mouths of the opponents, who asked what he meant by terrifying them with letters at a distance when he was another thing in their presence.

Reduce the possible readings to three and settle on the indicative as pressing home the charge, or agree in a line that either mood makes sense but the indicative the best, since they ought to look below the surface; say that the rivals valued themselves on external advantages and claimed peculiar honour because they were superior in personal appearance; suggest that the word rendered somewhat more is literally somewhat too much and may be quoted from a term the critics had used; hold it scarcely open to question that the authority claimed includes power to enforce itself by supernatural chastisement; read the boast as a claim that could be substantiated by higher evidence than has been urged; gloss the closing verb, that he will not be put to shame as a convicted impostor or pretentious boaster; supply the broken sentence with the connection, that he might boast more precisely so as not to seem to terrify by letters merely, or make the suppressed clause the substance of the threat, that the sentence he might pass will be no hollow form and he does not mean to frighten them as with a bugbear; and note the construction from the papyri, the rarity of the verb for frightening, and the plural in letters.

Narrow the indefinite pronoun to one man, the false apostle who had made so much disturbance in the church; leave that man to his own reflection before convincing him by a severer method; turn the verse into a rule of office, quoting an authority for the maxim that this is what pastors ever propose to themselves in exercising authority, and adding that it is employed for edification in righteousness and not for the destruction of any delinquent; call the next sentence elliptical and supply that he has not used this authority and will add no more on the point, lest he seem, as his adversary has insinuated, to wish to terrify them by his letters; or reduce the whole to five words, threatening more than I can perform.
Reason the case with those who despised him and spoke hardly of him, asking whether outward appearance is a fit measure by which to judge between him and his adversaries.

Stand back from the argument to admire its management, since what one may especially admire is that when he has fallen upon an urgent necessity for exalting himself he contrives both to do it and not to appear offensive to the many on account of the egotism, as may be seen particularly in another of his letters.

debates: Whether the opening verb is indicative, imperative or interrogative.
Who is meant by the indefinite any man.
What is to be supplied at the broken sentence.
What the plural letters implies.
outliers: Calvin alone lays out every ambiguity of the clause before choosing among them.
Chrysostom alone praises the management of a necessary self-praise, and alone compares another epistle for it.
Clarke alone identifies a single opponent behind the indefinite pronoun.
Ellicott alone suggests that the word for boasting is quoted back from the critics.
Gill alone lists the particulars by which the Apostle was judged.

10.pericope_label: His letters are weighty: the taunt quoted, and the folly of self-measurement

schools.summary: Mark what is singular here, that allusive references to what was said of him have appeared often but this is the first place where the very words are quoted, the scorn in them having wounded a sensitive nature like a poisoned arrow; report the manuscripts, the older Latin giving they say where the critical editors prefer a singular, says one, the leader; raise the ambiguity that the two adjectives can be uncomplimentary, meaning severe and violent rather than impressive and vigorous; have him contradict the charge outright, so that none may flatter themselves there will be any discrepancy between his words and deeds; keep to the pronoun, which asks not what nor who but what sort, so that his quality absent and present is precisely the same; change the tense and with it the force, supplying the present so that the sentence is less a threat of a particular instance than a statement of the settled character of his life; call the disclaimer a strain of severe but delicate irony; and hear a play on the two verbs, one meaning to insert or number among and the other to compare, adding that the half-playful assonance is hard to convey in English.

Reach the singular reading from the versions, since the Syriac and the Latin both point that way and one particular person seems to be in view whom he does not choose to name; take the quotation as the reason he had just declined to say more of his authority, so as to give the calumny no occasion; report that some read the disclaimer ironically, as though he would not pretend to put himself on a level with men of such gifts and learning and eloquence; and extend the stroke, since he afterwards does not merely compare himself boldly with them but derides their vanity and leaves them far behind, the blow falling not only on the boasters but on those who encouraged them by a misdirected approbation.

Fill out the sneer, that when you behold the man you find him a feeble and contemptible mortal and when you hear him speak his doctrine is good for nothing; pass on the tradition an early father gives for the bodily weakness, that his stature was low, his body crooked and his head bald; think the threat told, since it would doubtless have alarmed the false apostle, who very likely did not await the coming, being unwilling to try the fate of Elymas; call the disclaimer a strong irony and gloss the two verbs, to equal themselves as partners of the same office and to compare themselves as partakers of the same labour; and give the reason the method fails, that they are not sent of God nor inspired by his Spirit and so have no rule to think or act by, choosing and limiting their provinces by their own fancy.

Say that they took a wrong course to commend themselves in measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves among themselves, which was not wise, since they prided themselves on their own attainments.

debates: Whether the taunt is quoted from one man or from a party.
Whether the adjectives in it are complimentary or not.
Whether the reply is a threat or a statement of settled character.
What exactly is wrong with measuring oneself by oneself.
outliers: Ellicott alone marks this as the first place where the opponents' own words are quoted.
Robertson alone allows that the adjectives may mean severe and violent rather than impressive and vigorous.
Gill alone reaches the singular reading from the Syriac and the Latin.
Ellicott alone changes the tense so that the reply states a character rather than threatens an act.
Clarke alone supposes the man did not wait for the Apostle to arrive.
Wesley alone passes on the traditional description of the Apostle's person.

13.pericope_label: Within our measure: the rule God distributed, and other men's labours

schools.summary: Take the word for measure as an old term for a reed or measuring rod, common in the papyri for rules of every kind and the ancestor of our word canon, occurring only twice in the New Testament; give it instead a documentary sense, as the concordat established between this Apostle and one companion on the one side and three of the pillars on the other, whose terms he had not transgressed; find the obscurity in the brevity rather than the copies, and report an older English rendering, that we will not rejoice above measure; supply the particular variant, that some of the better manuscripts omit the negative, on which reading the sentence becomes a question, are we over-reaching as though you were not within the limit assigned us; note that the double compound verb for stretching too far seems to have been coined by the Apostle himself and turns up afterwards only in one late father; treat the charge of reaping another's harvest as a counter-charge, pressed home because it had first been brought against him; give the sequence plainly, that they came after he had been there and entered into his labours; and keep to the grammar of the closing clause, the genitive absolute in the growing of their faith and the passive of the verb for being magnified.

Make the measure a providential allotment, God having assigned each apostle his province and the bounds of it, and this one in particular the province of the Gentiles; turn it into a map, since they had not gone straight from Macedonia through Thessaly and across the Adriatic into Italy, which would have carried them past Corinth westward, but had left that direct path and come south through Greece into Achaia; warn that there is great difficulty in this verse and the three that follow, the manuscripts differing greatly so that the true reading can scarcely be determined; answer the charge in the language of the games, that they never attempted to enter into other men's labours but study to convert the regions assigned them by the Spirit, entering the course lawfully and running according to rule; and read the closing hope practically, that their faith being increased they can the better spare him and will enable him to go further still.

Say that they did not go beyond the bounds set by the purpose and providence of God in coming to Corinth; put the contrast rather than the definition, setting moderation against the presumption of the false apostles and finding the true measure of glorying in keeping within one's limits; describe the gesture behind the verb, of men who forcibly stretch out their arms or raise themselves on their feet to catch hold of what is not within reach; accuse the false apostles of putting their hand to the reaping of another man's harvest and then having the audacity to revile the men who had prepared a place for them at the cost of sweat and toil; and note that the disclaimer is repeated so that it may be explained.

debates: What the measure or rule consists in.
Whether the negative belongs in the text at the fourteenth verse.
Who was charged with building on another man's labours.
What the enlargement hoped for from their growth amounts to.
outliers: Ellicott alone identifies the measure with the agreement made at Jerusalem.
Clarke alone traces the actual route by which the Apostle reached Corinth.
Ellicott alone reports the manuscripts that omit the negative and turn the sentence into a question.
Robertson alone holds that the Apostle coined the compound verb himself.
Ellicott alone reads the charge of intrusion as one first made against the Apostle and then returned.

16.pericope_label: The regions beyond, and the glorying that is approved

schools.summary: Admit frankly that the destination can only be conjectured, offering other parts of Greece and passing on the suggestion that the gospel might travel by the trade of a commercial city; or settle it from the Apostle's own later words, which make it clear he is thinking of western Greece, of Rome and chiefly of Spain, where the gospel could be preached without any risk of its being said that he built on another man's foundation; contribute the word itself, a compound adverb meaning beyond those places, used as a preposition and found nowhere else outside the ecclesiastical writers; concede that boasting is not always improper, since the Apostle boasts elsewhere, only never of his own power or attainments; complain of translators who yield to their besetting weakness for variation by rendering one verb two ways; state the principle that a man is judged not by the estimate he places on himself but by the estimate God forms, a readiness to commend oneself being no evidence of salvation; gloss the word for approved as accepted, the Lord's own recommendation being what is accepted; and trace, here as at an earlier verse and in five passages before it, the impression the stinging taunt had left.

Look south to the Morea and west to Italy, adding that Africa does not appear to have been reckoned within the province, or say only that it means westward and southward where the gospel had not been preached; make the rule of glorying turn on the source of success, since none can succeed without the especial blessing of God, so that God who gave the blessing should have the glory and even a man commissioned immediately from God takes no praise to himself; and draw the portrait of the self-commender, who makes a parade of his own attainments, preaches himself and not Christ, and so far from being a servant for Christ's sake affects to be a ruler.

Hope that providence will direct into the more remote parts; say the maxim is added because the glorying just claimed might look like empty boasting, so that the Apostle cites himself and his rivals alike before the judgment-seat of God, where those glory on good grounds who are approved there; enumerate what is excluded from glorying — not oneself, nor outward circumstances, nor inward endowments, nor natural or acquired parts, nor wisdom or learning or eloquence, nor one's own righteousness and labours, much less other men's; define self-commendation as ascribing to oneself what does not belong to one, claiming to be a minister sent by Christ when one is not, or boasting of gifts one has not; and close on the practical difficulty, that it is easy to impose on men by a false impression and happens every day, so that we should aim exclusively at being approved by God and be satisfied with his approbation alone.

debates: Where the regions beyond are that the Apostle hoped to reach.
Whether boasting is ever proper, and on what terms.
What self-commendation consists in.
Whether the English version renders the verb for glorying consistently.
outliers: Ellicott alone settles the destination from the Apostle's own later statement, and alone names Spain as the chief object.
Barnes alone admits the destination is conjecture, and alone reports the guess that the gospel might travel by the city's trade.
Ellicott alone complains of the translators' weakness for variation, and alone counts the recurrences of the taunt through the chapter.
Gill alone enumerates the particulars a man is not to glory in.
Calvin alone brings both parties before the judgment seat to settle whose glorying has grounds.
